overview.text: Aluminum (Al; aluminium is an alternate spelling) is chemical element 13, a silvery-white, lightweight metal and the most abundant metal in Earth’s crust. It is rarely found as a pure metal in nature, so industry obtains it from bauxite: the Bayer process refines the ore into alumina, then the Hall–Héroult process uses electrolysis of alumina dissolved in molten cryolite to make aluminum. Its low density, ability to be shaped into thin sheets or wires, electrical conductivity, and resistance to corrosion make it useful in foil and cans, electrical lines, buildings, vehicles, and aircraft. Because pure aluminum is relatively soft, many structural parts use stronger aluminum alloys.

key_facts.text: Its chemical symbol is Al, and its atomic number is 13.
Aluminum is abundant in Earth’s crust but is usually bound in minerals rather than occurring as free metal.
Aluminum is malleable and ductile; its low density and corrosion resistance help make it useful in many applications.
Foil, cans, electrical transmission lines, building components, and aircraft parts are among its uses.
Primary production involves refining bauxite into alumina with the Bayer process, then using electrolysis in the Hall–Héroult process.
